t65z15a_st1p1w5p1: The words you use in this work point your attention somewhere. Unless the painful thing itself is what needs naming, pick words that point at what you're trying to strengthen, like an ability or a relationship, or something you want to do more of. Try telling yourself, "I'm not dependent." Where did your mind go just then? (Probably to "dependent.") "Let's help you build more ways to feel cared for and supported" usually gives it a clearer direction. With your little one, and in hypnosis especially, make that direction easy to picture: warmth, protection, steadiness, rest, or whatever's really needed.
t65z15a_st1p1w6p1: Words aim attention. If you tell yourself, "I'm not dependent on anyone," the word that sticks is "dependent." So unless the painful thing is what needs naming, aim the words at what you're building: the ability, the relationship, the thing you want to do more of. "Let's help you build more ways to feel cared for and supported" usually gives the mind a clearer direction than bringing in a label like "dependency" just to argue with it. In inner-child work and hypnosis especially, make it something you can picture (warmth, protection, steadiness, rest, whatever's really needed).
t65z15a_fg1p3w5p1: That doesn't make what they did harmless. In theory there were other options; they just weren't ones that person could reach by then. Punishing them can't go back and give them the awareness or support they were short on, or the ability. What's left is repairing what can be repaired, and making a different response easier to reach now. The harm is still real, and they're still accountable. Boundaries can still be right, and so can legal consequences, a moral judgment, distance, or cutting contact for good. You can understand someone, hold them responsible, never speak to them again and forgive them, all at once. "I understand how you became this way" can sit right next to "I now understand why I shouldn't rely on you for this."
t65z15a_secst34a:
Before giving anyone advice, your little one included, it can help to find out what kind of company they want: "Do you want me to mostly listen, help you untangle this, give you ideas, or some mix?" Not that you have to make a ritual of asking every time. If it's obvious what they want, go with that. If it isn't, that one sentence can keep you from advising somebody who's thinking, "I just need you to hear this." Or from just listening while they're asking for help thinking.

Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too. When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while. Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time's up, lends you the Protector. If you say no, they don't push. But they don't act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they're thinking, "Oh, I know what this is about," or "Here's what you should do." They keep it to themselves. A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you. Then you trade places.
